subject: Civil Engineering
title: Truss Bridges: Triangles Across Rivers
description: A quick, practical guide to Truss Bridges: Triangles Across Rivers.

hook.text: Railroad bridges needed to span farther and carry heavier loads. Trusses answered.

buildup.text: Trusses use triangular patterns so every member carries pure tension or compression.

discovery.text: Different truss types — Pratt, Howe, Warren — optimize for different load patterns.

twist.text: Trusses are deep but lightweight — more material at top and bottom where stress peaks.

climax.text: The Quebec Bridge spans 1,800 feet using a cantilever truss — the longest of its type.

punchline.text: Triangles made railways cross rivers the world over.

quiz.question: Why are all truss members in either pure tension or compression?
options: Special bolts at the joints prevent any bending
The triangular geometry ensures forces only pull or push each bar axially
Truss members are made from a material that cannot bend

details.summary: Truss bridges use connected triangular frameworks to distribute loads efficiently across a span. Because triangles are inherently rigid geometric shapes, trusses convert bending forces into axial tension and compression in individual members, making extremely efficient use of material.
details.whyItMatters: Trusses were the dominant bridge form during the railroad era and remain widely used today. Their efficiency makes them ideal when material economy and long spans are needed.
takeaways: Triangles are the only rigid polygon, making trusses inherently stable
Truss members carry only axial forces, either pure tension or compression
Common types include Pratt, Warren, and Howe trusses

faq.question: What is the difference between Pratt, Warren, and Howe trusses?
faq.answer: Pratt trusses have vertical members in compression and diagonal members in tension, ideal for steel. Warren trusses use alternating diagonal members without verticals, creating a clean zigzag pattern.

faq.question: Why were truss bridges so popular during the railroad expansion era?
faq.answer: Railroads needed bridges quickly at thousands of river crossings. Trusses could be prefabricated from standardized iron or steel members in factories, shipped by rail to the site, and assembled rapidly with minimal specialized equipment, making them ideal for rapid infrastructure expansion.
